sentences.show: Just after midnight on 6 June 1944, a glider with no engine crashed into a field in Normandy.
Its nose stopped in the German barbed wire, a few dozen meters from the bridge it had come to take.
Ten minutes later, both bridges were in British hands. This is the story of Pegasus Bridge.
Two bridges, 500 meters apart. One over the Caen Canal, one over the river Orne.
They were the only way east from Sword Beach, where British troops would land at dawn.
If the Germans blew them up, the British paratroopers on the far side would be cut off. If the Germans kept them, their tanks could drive straight to the beaches.
Intelligence said the bridges were guarded, and wired for demolition. There would be no time for a long fight.
So the plan was simple, and insane. Land right on top of them. In the dark. In gliders.
The job went to Major John Howard, a former policeman, and D Company of the Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire Light Infantry.
For weeks at a time they trained at night. They got up at 8 in the evening and went to bed at 1 in the afternoon.
They practised on two bridges in England that looked just like the real ones.
181 men, in six wooden gliders.
The lead pilot, Staff Sergeant Jim Wallwork, warned that the gliders were too heavy. Howard left men behind to make them lighter.
The code words for success were Ham, for the canal bridge, and Jam, for the river bridge.
At 10:56 PM on 5 June, Halifax bombers towed the gliders into the air from the south of England.
Over the French coast, the ropes were cut. The pilots flew on in silence, by compass and stopwatch.
At 00:16, Wallwork’s glider hit the ground, bounced across the field, and smashed into the barbed wire.
Both pilots were thrown through the cockpit glass. They were stunned, but alive.
Two more gliders landed a minute apart. One broke in half beside a pond. Lance Corporal Fred Greenhalgh was thrown into the water, and drowned.
On the bridge, two German sentries heard the noise. One ran, shouting “paratroops.” The other fired a flare.
Lieutenant Den Brotheridge led the first platoon across the bridge at a run.
A machine gun opened fire. Brotheridge threw a grenade, and was hit in the neck.
His men cleared the trenches and the pillbox with grenades and Sten guns. By 00:21, the canal bridge was theirs.
At the river bridge, one glider landed 300 meters away. A single mortar round knocked out the machine gun, and the platoon walked across.
Another glider was missing. It had landed by the wrong river, 13 kilometers away.
The engineers searched for the explosives. The bridges were ready to be blown, but the charges had never been put in place.
Howard’s radio operator sent the signal: Ham and Jam. Both bridges taken, intact.
Den Brotheridge died of his wounds. He is often called the first Allied soldier killed by enemy fire on D-Day.
His wife was 8 months pregnant. His daughter was born two weeks later.
Now they had to hold. Howard blew the letter V in Morse code on his whistle, to guide the paratroopers landing in the dark.
The German commander of the bridges drove onto them in a half-track to see what was happening. He was taken prisoner.
Around 2 AM, German tanks came down the road toward the bridge.
D Company had one working anti-tank weapon, a PIAT. Its first round hit the leading tank. The tank exploded, and the rest pulled back.
The big Panzer divisions could not move without Hitler’s order. Hitler was asleep, and his staff would not wake him.
At dawn came snipers. At 9, two German gunboats. At 10, a single plane dropped a bomb, which hit the bridge, and did not explode.
Then, at 1:30 PM, the men on the bridge heard bagpipes.
It was Bill Millin, the piper of Lord Lovat’s commandos, marching up from Sword Beach. The relief had arrived.
Legend says Lovat apologised for being a few minutes late. By the plan, they were well over an hour late.
Of the 181 men who landed, two were killed and 14 wounded.
Air Chief Marshal Leigh-Mallory called the landings among the most outstanding flying achievements of the war.
Howard received the Distinguished Service Order from Montgomery himself. Eight of the glider pilots got the Distinguished Flying Medal.
The canal bridge was renamed Pegasus Bridge, after the winged horse on the badge of the British airborne troops.
Every 6 June until he died, John Howard came back to lay a wreath where the gliders had landed.
So, was Pegasus Bridge won by perfect planning, or by perfect luck? Tell us what you think.
Their signal was Ham and Jam. Yours is a single tap on subscribe.
